newsitem.title: ANGOLA: Angola reaches milestone in clearing landmines.
newsitem.headline: Angola reaches milestone in clearing landmines.

text.p: Angola has reached a milestone in efforts to deal with its civil war landmine legacy by clearing mines from roads leading to all provincial capitals but one, a U.N. official said.
"Since September 30 all provincial capitals can be reached by road," U.N. chief of engineers Lieutenant-Colonel Froes de Moraes told Reuters this week.
But he added: "Around the town of Andulo, UNITA has refused to allow us in to demine the roads."
Andulo is close to Bailundo, headquarters of the UNITA opposition movement which signed a peace pact with the government two years ago.
An estimated 10 to 12 million landmines were planted during decades of war in Angola, which fought an independence struggle against Portugal until 1975 and then plunged into civil war.
The South African company Mechem Consultants Ltd began 15 months ago to clear mines from some 5,000 km (3,100 miles) of roads linking the capital Luanda with major towns in the interior.
"There has been some remining of roads by both sides from mid-July to mid-August," de Moraes said. "But it seems to have stopped now."
Mechem is now demining the last 100 km (60 mile) stretch of highway linking Luanda to Soyo, the oil city on the northern coast which is currently accessible only by air.

In Quinzau, on the road to Soyo, a local fisherman said: "Many people fled during the war. We survived by praying to God... we have been living with many difficulties. Everything will be easier with the road."
Mechem is using a mine-clearing method designed to complete the task with the minimum of fuss.
Mechem technicians, working under the protection of vehicles designed to withstand mine explosions, use machines which work like vacuum cleaners to gather air samples along the road.
These are sent to company headquarters in Lubango where sniffer dogs test them for the tell-tale vapours given off by explosives.
If a sample tests positive, teams equipped with conventional mine detectors comb the area where the sample was gathered.
"With our system we cover only the area which tests positive," said Mechem quality assurance chief Rocky van Blerk said.
"Our contract states that the system has to have a 99.6 percent guarantee of safety."
